name: Cognitive Psychology
description: An in-depth exploration of mental processes including attention, perception, memory, language, problem solving, and decision making. Students examine classic experiments and contemporary research to understand how the mind organizes, stores, and retrieves information.

modules.title: History of Cognitive Psychology
modules.objectives: Trace the cognitive revolution from behaviorism to information-processing models; identify key figures including Neisser, Miller, and Broadbent. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — History of Psychology — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — History of Cognitive Psychology (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Chapter 1 summary — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Build an evidence timeline with four entries: behaviorism’s emphasis on observable behavior; Miller’s 1956 work on information capacity; Broadbent’s 1958 filter model; Neisser’s 1967 synthesis of cognitive psychology. For each entry, explain the contribution and one link to the information-processing approach. Then write a 250–300 word claim explaining why the cognitive revolution changed what psychologists could study without claiming behaviorism disappeared. Submit: timeline and claim. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: chronology 25%, conceptual accuracy 40%, evidence-based explanation 35%.

modules.title: Perception & Attention
modules.objectives: Explain selective, divided, and sustained attention; describe bottleneck theories; apply findings from the cocktail party effect and change blindness.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — Sensation versus Perception — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Perception & Attention (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Chapter 5 summary — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Analyze this fictional attention dataset; do not test people. In condition A (count passes), 24 of 40 viewers noticed an unexpected red umbrella. In condition B (watch freely), 36 of 40 noticed it. Meanwhile, a listener detects their name in 7 of 20 unattended-message trials. Calculate both noticing percentages and the 12-person difference, then write 250–300 words using selective attention, inattentional blindness, and the cocktail-party effect. State one limitation: these summary data cannot diagnose any individual’s attention. Submit: a single labeled document containing every required artifact. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: calculations 25%, theory application 45%, limitation 15%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Memory Systems
modules.objectives: Distinguish sensory, short-term, and long-term memory; compare the Atkinson-Shiffrin model with Baddeley's working memory model. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — How Memory Functions — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Memory Systems (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Chapter 8 summary — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Create a diagram comparing the Atkinson–Shiffrin model with Baddeley’s working-memory model. Your diagram must label sensory memory, short-term memory, long-term memory, central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer. Add arrows showing information flow, then write 200–250 words explaining two similarities and two differences. Submit: diagram and explanation. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: accurate components 40%, relationships 30%, comparison 30%.

modules.title: Working Memory
modules.objectives: Describe Baddeley's components of working memory (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer, central executive); explain its role in reasoning and comprehension.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — Working memory in How Memory Functions
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Working Memory (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Memory model review — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional task record; do not measure yourself or anyone else: Trial 1 repeats digits 4-9-2 correctly; Trial 2 repeats 7-1-8-3 correctly; Trial 3 repeats 6-2-9-4-1 correctly; Trial 4 misses 8-3-1-7-5-2. During a second task, recalling six short words is correct but six long multisyllabic words has two errors. Explain the pattern with the phonological loop, central executive, capacity limits, and word-length effect. Submit: a 300-word analysis plus a labeled working-memory diagram. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: evidence use 30%, model accuracy 45%, non-diagnostic limitation 10%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Long-term Memory
modules.objectives: Differentiate explicit (declarative: episodic and semantic) from implicit (procedural, priming) memory; explain consolidation and the role of the hippocampus.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — Brain Systems and Memory — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Long-term Memory (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Long-term memory review — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Classify these fictional examples as episodic, semantic, or procedural memory and justify each: remembering a graduation ceremony, knowing Ottawa is Canada’s capital, typing without looking, recalling yesterday’s lunch, knowing what “photosynthesis” means, and tying a bowline knot. Then explain how explicit and implicit memory differ and identify the likely role of the hippocampus in forming new explicit memories. Submit: classification table and 250-word explanation. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: classifications 35%, justification 30%, systems explanation 35%.

modules.title: Forgetting
modules.objectives: Explain Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve; distinguish decay theory from interference theory; describe retrieval failure and motivated forgetting. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — Problems with Memory — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Forgetting (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Ways to Enhance Memory — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Analyze this provided retention record; do not track your own performance: 20 terms learned, then 15 recalled after 20 minutes, 11 after one day, 9 after two days, and 8 after three days. Plot or tabulate percent retained, describe the curve, and compare decay, interference, and retrieval failure as explanations. Propose a three-session spaced-practice plan and explain why the pattern alone cannot prove which mechanism caused forgetting. Submit: table/graph and 300-word analysis. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: calculations 25%, theory comparison 40%, evidence limits 20%, study plan 15%.

modules.title: Mental Imagery
modules.objectives: Describe mental rotation and image scanning research; evaluate whether mental images are pictorial or propositional; apply imagery to memory enhancement.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — What Is Cognition? — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Mental Imagery (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Cognition chapter summary — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Use the provided mental-rotation results: mean response time is 1.2 seconds at 0°, 1.8 at 60°, 2.4 at 120°, and 3.0 at 180°, with accuracy 94%, 92%, 88%, and 83%. Create a graph, describe both trends, explain how the response-time pattern supports an analog/spatial account, and give one propositional alternative. Do not take an online ability test or infer an individual trait. Submit: graph and 250–300 word analysis. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: graph/data accuracy 30%, competing explanations 45%, limits 25%.

modules.title: Language & Thought
modules.objectives: Explain the structure of language (phonemes, morphemes, syntax, semantics); evaluate the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis; describe Chomsky's universal grammar. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e — Language — use this reading to check the module concepts and examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Language & Thought (current public lesson video).
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax — Language and thought review — use this source to review and apply the module concepts.
modules.assignment: Compare two interpretations of this fictional result: speakers of Language A, which uses separate basic terms for light and dark blue, sort cross-category blue pairs 80 ms faster than same-category pairs; speakers of Language B show a 20 ms difference. Write a 300-word analysis distinguishing strong linguistic determinism from weaker linguistic relativity. Include phoneme, morpheme, syntax, and semantics in a short concept table, and state two alternative explanations or design limitations. Submit: table and analysis. Include: use the provided facts or data as evidence and explain how each major choice applies a module concept. Evaluation: conceptual accuracy 40%, evidence reasoning 35%, limitations 25%.

quizQuestions.question: The cognitive revolution emerged primarily as a reaction against:
quizQuestions.answer: Behaviorism
quizQuestions.explanation: The cognitive revolution in the 1950s-60s was a rejection of behaviorism's exclusive focus on observable behavior.

quizQuestions.question: George Miller's famous 1956 paper identified short-term memory capacity as approximately:
quizQuestions.answer: 7 items (plus or minus 2)
quizQuestions.explanation: Miller's 'Magic Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' described the limited capacity of short-term memory.

quizQuestions.question: Which development made internal mental processes easier to study scientifically?
options: Using information-processing models with testable predictions
Treating every behavior as a reflex
quizQuestions.answer: Using information-processing models with testable predictions
quizQuestions.explanation: Information-processing models represented mental operations in ways that generated observable, testable predictions. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: In selective attention research, what does the cocktail party effect illustrate?
options: Selective attention to relevant stimuli in a noisy environment
The inability to process two conversations simultaneously
quizQuestions.answer: Selective attention to relevant stimuli in a noisy environment
quizQuestions.explanation: The cocktail party effect shows we can selectively attend to our name even in a crowded, noisy setting.

quizQuestions.question: In Perception & Attention, Change blindness refers to:
options: The inability to perceive color changes
Failure to notice large changes in a scene when attention is elsewhere
A medical condition affecting peripheral vision
quizQuestions.answer: Failure to notice large changes in a scene when attention is elsewhere
quizQuestions.explanation: Change blindness demonstrates that we do not automatically encode all aspects of a visual scene.

quizQuestions.question: The inattentional blindness experiment by Simons and Chabris showed:
options: Observers miss unexpected objects when focused on a primary task
Vision is processed entirely in parallel
quizQuestions.answer: Observers miss unexpected objects when focused on a primary task
quizQuestions.explanation: When focused on counting basketball passes, many participants failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through.

quizQuestions.question: In Broadbent's early-selection model, the filter first selects information using:
options: Physical features such as channel or voice pitch
Full semantic meaning of every message
The emotional value of all unattended words
quizQuestions.answer: Physical features such as channel or voice pitch
quizQuestions.explanation: Broadbent proposed an early filter that selects one channel using physical characteristics before full semantic analysis; unattended channels are largely blocked.

quizQuestions.question: Sensory memory holds information for approximately:
options: Less than a second to a few seconds
quizQuestions.answer: Less than a second to a few seconds
quizQuestions.explanation: Sensory memory (iconic and echoic) holds exact copies of sensory input for very brief durations before it decays.

quizQuestions.question: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model is also known as the:
quizQuestions.answer: Multi-store model
quizQuestions.explanation: Atkinson and Shiffrin's 1968 model proposed three distinct memory stores: sensory, short-term, and long-term. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Rehearsal in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model serves to:
options: Transfer information from STM to LTM
quizQuestions.answer: Transfer information from STM to LTM
quizQuestions.explanation: Maintenance rehearsal recirculates information in STM; elaborative rehearsal encodes it into LTM. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: The phonological loop in Baddeley's working memory model handles:
quizQuestions.answer: Verbal and auditory information
quizQuestions.explanation: The phonological loop temporarily stores and rehearses verbal/auditory information (like repeating a phone number).

quizQuestions.question: The central executive in Baddeley's model functions as:
options: The sole source of memory capacity
quizQuestions.answer: An attentional controller coordinating subsystems
quizQuestions.explanation: The central executive directs attention and controls the slave systems (phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad).

quizQuestions.question: The word-length effect demonstrates that:
options: Working memory capacity is affected by how long words take to say
Short words are harder to chunk
Rehearsal does not help working memory
quizQuestions.answer: Working memory capacity is affected by how long words take to say
quizQuestions.explanation: Longer words take more time to rehearse, reducing the number that can be held in the phonological loop.

quizQuestions.question: The episodic buffer in Baddeley's model was added to account for:
options: The integration of information across modalities into coherent episodes
quizQuestions.answer: The integration of information across modalities into coherent episodes
quizQuestions.explanation: Added in 2000, the episodic buffer integrates information from the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and LTM into unified episodes.

quizQuestions.question: Episodic memory contains memories of:
quizQuestions.answer: Personal autobiographical events
quizQuestions.explanation: Episodic memory stores personally experienced events with their temporal and spatial context. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Priming is best classified as:
quizQuestions.answer: Implicit memory
quizQuestions.explanation: Priming — a prior exposure facilitating later processing — is an implicit, unconscious form of memory. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Which example is semantic memory?
options: Knowing that water freezes at 0°C under standard pressure
Showing faster recognition after an unnoticed prime
quizQuestions.answer: Knowing that water freezes at 0°C under standard pressure
quizQuestions.explanation: Semantic memory stores general facts and concepts rather than autobiographical episodes or skills. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Which brain structure is especially important for forming new explicit memories?
quizQuestions.answer: Hippocampus
quizQuestions.explanation: The hippocampus is central to forming new explicit memories, as evidence from patient H.M. helped show.

quizQuestions.question: What pattern did Ebbinghaus observe in memory retention over time?
options: Rapid initially then slowing over time
quizQuestions.answer: Rapid initially then slowing over time
quizQuestions.explanation: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows steep initial forgetting that decelerates as time passes. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Proactive interference occurs when:
options: New memories interfere with old ones
Old memories interfere with new learning
quizQuestions.answer: Old memories interfere with new learning
quizQuestions.explanation: Proactive interference: old information makes it harder to learn or remember new information. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Retrograde amnesia results in:
options: Loss of memories prior to brain injury
quizQuestions.answer: Loss of memories prior to brain injury
quizQuestions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia causes loss of memories formed before the injury, while anterograde amnesia affects new memory formation.

quizQuestions.question: A student learns Spanish vocabulary, then newly learned Italian words disrupt recall of the Spanish words. This is:
quizQuestions.answer: Retroactive interference
quizQuestions.explanation: Newer information interfering with older information is retroactive interference. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Shepard and Metzler's mental rotation experiments showed that:
options: Images are stored in verbal codes
Rotation time increases linearly with the angle of rotation
Visual imagery uses different brain areas than perception
quizQuestions.answer: Rotation time increases linearly with the angle of rotation
quizQuestions.explanation: Response time increased proportionally with the degree of rotation, suggesting people mentally rotate images in a continuous, analog way.

quizQuestions.question: The pictorial view of mental imagery (Kosslyn) proposes that:
options: Images are stored as abstract propositions
Mental images are depictive, spatial representations
Images are reconstructed from semantic memory
quizQuestions.answer: Mental images are depictive, spatial representations
quizQuestions.explanation: Kosslyn argued mental images are quasi-pictorial, activating visual cortex areas similar to actual perception. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Accuracy falls as angular difference grows, while response time rises. Which conclusion is most cautious?
options: The task proves a fixed spatial ability trait
The pattern is consistent with a mental transformation that takes more time at larger angles
The images must be stored only as words
Response time cannot inform theories of imagery
quizQuestions.answer: The pattern is consistent with a mental transformation that takes more time at larger angles
quizQuestions.explanation: The data support an analog transformation account but do not diagnose a fixed individual ability.

quizQuestions.question: A morpheme is best defined as:
options: The smallest unit of sound in a language
The smallest unit of meaning in a language
The meaning of a word in context
quizQuestions.answer: The smallest unit of meaning in a language
quizQuestions.explanation: Morphemes are the smallest linguistic units that carry meaning (e.g., 'un-', 'happy', '-ness'). The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

quizQuestions.question: Chomsky's universal grammar hypothesis states that:
options: All languages share the same vocabulary roots
Humans have an innate capacity for language structure
Only spoken language follows grammar rules
quizQuestions.answer: Humans have an innate capacity for language structure
quizQuestions.explanation: Chomsky proposed that all humans are biologically equipped with a universal grammar framework for language acquisition.

quizQuestions.question: The strong Sapir-Whorf hypothesis would mean that:
options: Language has no effect on thought
Speakers of different languages perceive reality differently due to their language
Thought develops before language in children
quizQuestions.answer: Speakers of different languages perceive reality differently due to their language
quizQuestions.explanation: The strong Sapir-Whorf hypothesis posits that the language we speak determines how we think and perceive the world.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement reflects weak linguistic relativity rather than strong determinism?
options: Language completely prevents thoughts without matching words
Language can influence attention or categorization without fully determining thought
All languages produce identical cognitive patterns
Grammar makes perception impossible to study
quizQuestions.answer: Language can influence attention or categorization without fully determining thought
quizQuestions.explanation: Weak linguistic relativity allows language to bias some cognitive processes without controlling what people can think.

questions.question: The cognitive revolution was primarily a reaction against which school of psychology?
questions.answer: Behaviorism
questions.explanation: The cognitive revolution in the 1950s-60s rejected behaviorism's exclusive focus on observable behavior, reintroducing mental processes as scientific subjects.

questions.question: George Miller's 'magic number' for short-term memory capacity is approximately:
questions.answer: 7 items (plus or minus 2)
questions.explanation: Miller found that short-term memory holds approximately 7 (plus or minus 2) chunks of information.

questions.question: The cocktail party effect demonstrates:
options: Inability to attend to any background noise
Selective attention to one's name in a noisy environment
Parallel processing of all auditory stimuli
The limit of working memory capacity
questions.answer: Selective attention to one's name in a noisy environment
questions.explanation: The cocktail party effect shows we selectively filter relevant stimuli (like our name) even while attending to other things.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? The central executive in Baddeley's working memory model serves as:
options: An attentional controller coordinating the subsystems
A permanent store for all autobiographical memories
The speech muscles used in rehearsal
A sensory receptor for visual input
questions.answer: An attentional controller coordinating the subsystems
questions.explanation: The central executive allocates attention and coordinates the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer.

questions.question: Sperling's partial report procedure showed that iconic memory:
options: Holds more information than can be fully recalled
questions.answer: Holds more information than can be fully recalled
questions.explanation: By cuing participants to report specific rows after stimulus offset, Sperling showed iconic memory holds more than participants can fully report.

questions.question: Encoding specificity states that recall is best when:
questions.answer: Retrieval context matches encoding context
questions.explanation: Tulving's encoding specificity: memory is strongest when the conditions at retrieval match those present during encoding.

questions.question: Shepard and Metzler's mental rotation studies suggested that mental images are:
options: Not processed in the visual system
questions.answer: Analog and spatially represented
questions.explanation: Rotation time increased linearly with angle of rotation, suggesting mental images behave like physical objects being rotated.

questions.question: In an early-selection account of attention, unattended information is filtered primarily on the basis of:
options: Its emotional value after conscious analysis
questions.answer: Its physical features
questions.explanation: Broadbent’s early-filter model proposes selection based on physical features before full semantic processing. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Chomsky's universal grammar proposes that:
options: All languages share identical grammar rules
Children have an innate predisposition to acquire language structure
questions.answer: Children have an innate predisposition to acquire language structure
questions.explanation: Chomsky proposed a biologically innate language acquisition device that provides children with a universal grammar framework.

questions.question: The case of patient H.M. demonstrated that the hippocampus is critical for:
questions.answer: Forming new explicit memories
questions.explanation: After bilateral hippocampal removal, H.M. could not form new declarative (explicit) memories. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows that forgetting is:
options: Most rapid shortly after learning then slowing
Faster for emotionally neutral material only
questions.answer: Most rapid shortly after learning then slowing
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus showed that the most forgetting occurs shortly after learning, with the rate slowing as time progresses.

questions.question: Which finding most directly demonstrates inattentional blindness?
options: People recall more after spaced practice
Observers counting passes fail to notice an unexpected object
questions.answer: Observers counting passes fail to notice an unexpected object
questions.explanation: Focusing attention on one task can cause observers to miss a visible, unexpected stimulus. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly represents the Atkinson–Shiffrin model?
questions.answer: Sensory → short-term → long-term
questions.explanation: The multi-store model describes information moving from sensory memory to short-term memory and, with encoding or rehearsal, to long-term memory.

questions.question: Which component of Baddeley’s model temporarily maintains visual and spatial information?
questions.answer: Visuospatial sketchpad
questions.explanation: The visuospatial sketchpad maintains visual and spatial information in working memory. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which comparison between the Atkinson–Shiffrin and Baddeley models is accurate?
options: Both treat short-term processing as a single store with no subsystems
Baddeley divides working memory into coordinated components, while Atkinson–Shiffrin treats short-term memory as a store
questions.answer: Baddeley divides working memory into coordinated components, while Atkinson–Shiffrin treats short-term memory as a store
questions.explanation: The models differ especially in how they describe active short-term processing. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? The testing effect demonstrates that:
options: Re-reading is the most effective study strategy
Testing works only for motor skills
questions.answer: Retrieval practice strengthens later retention
questions.explanation: The testing effect shows that actively retrieving information improves later memory. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Loftus's misinformation effect research showed that:
options: Memory is immune to post-event suggestion
Leading questions can alter eyewitness memories
Emotional events are always remembered accurately
Repressed memories can be reliably recovered
questions.answer: Leading questions can alter eyewitness memories
questions.explanation: Loftus demonstrated that misleading post-event information can become incorporated into eyewitness memory. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Spaced practice is superior to massed practice because:
options: It forces repeated retrieval over time strengthening long-term retention
questions.answer: It forces repeated retrieval over time strengthening long-term retention
questions.explanation: Spaced practice distributes learning across time, requiring retrieval from progressively longer intervals, which consolidates memory.

questions.question: A witness’s later memory changes after reading a misleading description. This illustrates:
questions.answer: The misinformation effect
questions.explanation: Post-event information can alter later recollection, demonstrating reconstructive memory. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? Priming is classified as implicit memory because:
options: It influences behavior without requiring conscious awareness
It requires deliberate recall of an event
It is always a verbal memory
It depends only on working memory capacity
questions.answer: It influences behavior without requiring conscious awareness
questions.explanation: Priming can affect perception or behavior even when the person is not consciously recalling the earlier stimulus.

questions.question: Which study plan best applies retrieval practice?
options: Reread notes repeatedly without checking recall
Close the notes, answer questions from memory, then check feedback
Copy definitions while looking at them
questions.answer: Close the notes, answer questions from memory, then check feedback
questions.explanation: Retrieval practice requires attempting to recall information, followed by feedback to correct errors. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: The word-length effect in working memory shows that:
options: Longer words are easier to remember
Fewer long words can be held in the phonological loop than short words
Word length affects only semantic memory
Working memory capacity is unlimited for familiar words
questions.answer: Fewer long words can be held in the phonological loop than short words
questions.explanation: Long words take longer to subvocally rehearse, reducing the number that can be maintained in the phonological loop.

questions.question: Which schedule best exemplifies spaced practice?
options: Three one-hour sessions across several days
Reading the same page three times immediately
questions.answer: Three one-hour sessions across several days
questions.explanation: Spacing distributes practice over time, producing repeated encoding and retrieval opportunities. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? Retrograde amnesia involves:
options: Loss of memories from before the onset of amnesia
Inability to form new long-term memories
questions.answer: Loss of memories from before the onset of amnesia
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia concerns memories formed before the injury or onset; anterograde amnesia concerns forming new memories.

questions.question: The method of loci memory technique leverages:
options: Spatial mental imagery linked to a familiar route
questions.answer: Spatial mental imagery linked to a familiar route
questions.explanation: The method of loci encodes information by placing mental images along a well-known spatial route, exploiting spatial memory strengths.

questions.question: Which pattern best matches the typical forgetting curve?
options: A steep early decline followed by slower loss
No loss until one week passes
questions.answer: A steep early decline followed by slower loss
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus observed that forgetting is often fastest soon after learning and then slows. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which observation supports retrieval failure rather than permanent loss?
options: A forgotten answer returns when the original context is restored
New learning erases every old memory
A skill can never be performed again
Recognition and recall are always identical
questions.answer: A forgotten answer returns when the original context is restored
questions.explanation: Recovery with an effective cue suggests the information remained stored but was temporarily inaccessible. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? Broadbent's filter model of attention proposes that:
options: A selective filter blocks most information based on physical characteristics early in processing
All unattended information is fully processed for meaning
questions.answer: A selective filter blocks most information based on physical characteristics early in processing
questions.explanation: Broadbent's early-selection model proposes filtering based on physical features before full semantic processing. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: The dual-coding theory (Paivio) suggests that memory is improved when information is:
options: Encoded in both verbal and visual/imagistic codes
questions.answer: Encoded in both verbal and visual/imagistic codes
questions.explanation: Paivio's dual-coding theory states that information encoded both verbally and visually creates richer, more retrievable memory traces.

questions.question: Which result would most strongly support an analog account of mental rotation?
options: Response time increases roughly with angular disparity
Every angle produces the same response time
questions.answer: Response time increases roughly with angular disparity
questions.explanation: A graded time cost with larger rotations is consistent with spatial transformation of a depictive representation.

questions.question: Which claim is the safest interpretation of a group mental-rotation result?
options: It diagnoses each participant’s fixed ability
It describes an average task pattern and does not by itself diagnose individuals
It proves imagery is entirely pictorial
questions.answer: It describes an average task pattern and does not by itself diagnose individuals
questions.explanation: Group averages support claims about the observed task and sample, not clinical or fixed-trait conclusions about individuals.

questions.question: A phoneme differs from a morpheme because a phoneme is:
options: A basic sound unit, while a morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit
questions.answer: A basic sound unit, while a morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit
questions.explanation: Phonemes distinguish sounds; morphemes carry meaning. The other choices do not fit the evidence, definition, or communication purpose given in the prompt.

questions.question: A student first learns route A, then route B. On a route B test, details from route A intrude. Which explanation fits best?
questions.answer: Proactive interference
questions.explanation: Previously learned route A interferes with recall of the newer route B, which is proactive interference.

questions.question: Sapir-Whorf (linguistic relativity) research on color perception suggests:
options: Having more color terms in a language speeds discrimination between those colors
questions.answer: Having more color terms in a language speeds discrimination between those colors
questions.explanation: Research shows that fine-grained linguistic color categories can facilitate faster perceptual discrimination between colors in those categories.

questions.question: The episodic buffer in Baddeley's working memory model was added to explain:
options: Visual manipulation of objects in mental space
Integration of information from multiple sources into coherent episodes
The capacity limits of sensory memory
questions.answer: Integration of information from multiple sources into coherent episodes
questions.explanation: The episodic buffer integrates information from the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into unified, multi-modal episodes.
